newsitem.title: UK: Gold Council says Australia sale "unnecessary".
newsitem.headline: Gold Council says Australia sale "unnecessary".

text.p: The Geneva-based World Gold Council (WGC) described on Friday as "unnecessary" and lacking "sensitivity" the sale by the Reserve Bank of Australia of 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves announced the previous day.
"We have made this statement at the request of our members in Australia," said the WGC's chief executive E.M. Hood in a telephone interview.
The gold price which had been weakening under a combination of negative factors collapsed to 12-year lows after the Australain news hit the market.
Gold closed on Friday at $324.25/$324.75 about $7.00 under its Thursday close which was before the bulk of the selling.

"For a leading gold producer to take unnecessary actions that prejudice the well being of a key sector of its economy suggest a lack of sensitivity to the factors impacting the market," the WGC's statement said.
Hood said the impact of the Australian decision on the gold price was "very serious" for his member companies.
"Many are unhedged and a lot of big companies are under pressure," he said.
He added that a low gold price was also serious for gold consumers in developing countries where hoarding bullion in the form of small bars or jewellery was often the only means of saving.

"This action appears to have been motivated by narrow financial considerations. The Austrsalian public needs to be aware that it will have wider negative consequences for the Australian economy," the WGC said in its statement.
The WGC is a gold promotional organisation sponsored by many of the world's leading gold producers.
Hood noted that the WGC itself was under pressure at these prices.
"The one positive in the future is the strength of underlying demand for jewellery," he said.
But he added that the WGC's promotional work could be jeopardised if it did not have the funding from the mining companies.
The WGC members pay $2.50 per ounce of gold sold to the council and new memebrs pay $1.00 for the first two years of their membership.
Hood said there is a hardship catogory of membership which allows companies to pay a lower subscription if their profitability falls to a set level.
"We have members in the hardship category now and I expect more will be applying for it at these prices," he said.
